source.title: When Worse is Better: Navigating the compression-generation tradeoff in visual tokenization
source.authors: V. Ramanujan; Kushal Tirumala; Armen Aghajanyan; Luke S. Zettlemoyer; Ali Farhadi

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure text is garbled, but the relevant findings are described in the paper text.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in autoregressive image generation and reports that the observed scaling and compute-efficient tokenization depend on the tokenizer and regime, including departures near performance saturation. This refines how broadly a single scaling law applies.
record.gate_note: The paper tests scaling for visual-token validation cross-entropy and image-generation FID, not language-model pretraining loss. Rows below concern the image-modality and setup-dependence versions only. Comparisons and numerical results from cited prior work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study fits compute scaling laws for autoregressive visual-token models on ImageNet, from 52M to 775M parameters over about four orders of training FLOPs. It reports power-law fits for validation cross-entropy and gFID, and shows that the fitted exponents change with tokenizer choices and that curves deviate near saturation. This is a new setting (image modality, repeated data) with results on V5 and V7. T3 fits better than T5, since the paper does not argue that any version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that the compression–generation trade-off depends on stage-2 capacity: smaller models benefit from more aggressive compression even at worse reconstruction. Scaling laws show consistent patterns across orders of magnitude of compute. CRT improves compute efficiency 2–3× and parameter efficiency ~4×, with gains largest at small scale. The paraphrase should add that more tokens per image only become compute-optimal near the rFID floor.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies autoregressive visual-token modeling and image-generation metrics, not language-model held-out text loss. It uses ImageNet and LSUN and varies image-tokenizer rate and causal regularization.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling results depend on visual tokenization choices: sequence length, codebook size, and CRT versus baseline. Sequence-length advantages change near the reconstruction-FID barrier; the 1k versus 131k codebook ordering reverses between low and high compute. The study uses repeated data and a cosine learning-rate schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation loss predicts gFID ordering only when training steps are held constant. Overtrained models reach lower gFID at higher loss, but the compute-Pareto frontiers of loss and gFID coincide (Section 3.3.1, Figure 4 right).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In image AR models, pretraining loss predicts generation quality only along the compute-optimal frontier or at fixed step count.

fits_no_version.finding: gFID power-law fits from the sweep are extrapolated (Figure 5/6 'Extrapolation' lines). The true trend deviates more from the prediction as tokens per image grow near saturation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extrapolation of generation-metric scaling fits breaks down near the irreducible reconstruction floor.

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025), as stated in the paper text; venue metadata supplied as arXiv.org.
record.problems: The largest tested stage 2 model is 775M parameters. The authors identify finite ImageNet data and repeated-data training as limitations, and primarily use class-to-image synthesis. The evidence concerns image-generation and visual-token losses rather than language-model loss. No error bars or confidence intervals are reported in the text for the scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: No separately tabulated individual-run values were transcribed from scaling plots. Rows record the aggregate scaling statements and setup-dependent comparisons described in the text and figure captions.

untested.parts: Language-model text pretraining loss is not studied. The study only reports compute scaling for visual tokens. Parameter-only and data-only scaling laws are not fitted (Figure 10 shows data size only qualitatively).
Language-model extrapolation is not tested. The image-model gFID extrapolation lines are noted under fits_no_version.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is fitted.
Depth/width at fixed parameter count is not varied.

Video, audio, fine-tuning and transfer regimes are not tested. Parameter and data power laws in images are not fitted separately. Scale stops at 775M parameters, and the setting is repeated-data ImageNet only.
Downstream task performance is not measured.
Parameter-counting conventions and fitting methods are not compared. There is no comparison of published language-model laws.

missing.what: Fitted gFID Pareto exponents and floors per tokens-per-image: 256: 0.65, +2.21; 400: 0.54, +1.3; 576: 0.58, +0.99; all R²=0.99
Fitted gFID Pareto exponents per codebook size: 1k: 0.67 (R²=0.98, floor 2.7); 16k: 0.64 (floor 2.21); 131k: 0.57 (floor 1.78)
Validation-loss power-law exponents: baseline 0.255, CRT 0.264 (R²=0.99), fitted without an irreducible term
Validation loss vs dataset size (1e7–1e8+ tokens) for 111M–775M models at 250k iterations. Used to argue there is no data bottleneck; no fit is reported

record.verdict_notes: The study is not one of the original sources. Exponents are read from figure legends where minus signs were lost in extraction. Training compute is swept by iteration count with cosine schedules, evaluating separate runs' endpoints, on repeated ImageNet data (~3e8 tokens). CRT vs baseline comparisons (R7, R9, Table 1, LSUN) evaluate the authors' method and are not scaling-law tests.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments use visual tokens and image generation, not held-out text-pretraining loss in language models.
The study does not test whether small language-model runs predict much larger language-model runs.
It studies image-token sequence length and compute, but does not measure compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as stable powers of compute.
The study does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture changes at fixed parameter count as a test of loss sensitivity.
Tests image token modeling and image generation, including repeated-data ImageNet training and LSUN evaluation. Does not test video, audio, fine-tuning or transfer as scaling regimes.
Generation FID is not a downstream-task performance measure. The paper does not test downstream-task improvement as a function of pretraining loss or scale.

Shows setup-dependent scaling behavior for visual tokenizers, including effects of token count, codebook size, and CRT. Does not compare parameter-counting conventions or alternative fitting procedures, or establish disagreement between published language-model laws.

rows.subject: Stage 2 autoregressive image-generation models (aggregate Pareto frontier; ImageNet 256x256)
rows.size_stated: Models in the sweep range from 5.21 × 10^7 to 7.75 × 10^8 parameters.
rows.stage_stated: Stage 2 autoregressive generation; independently trained runs, evaluated at their endpoints.
rows.operation_detail: Swept training compute and measured validation cross-entropy loss using a fixed stage 1 tokenizer.
rows.measure: Validation cross-entropy loss versus training FLOPs; authors report consistent log-log-linear scaling on the compute validation-loss Pareto curve.
rows.value: Consistent log-log-linear scaling across four orders of magnitude; no exact validation-loss exponent stated in the text.
rows.note: The paper reports the result for the Pareto curve across model scales, rather than giving a separate numerical loss value for each run in the text.
rows.check: The value is wrong: the exponent is stated in Figure 4 (left). The Pareto fit is L = C^0.255·e^8.622 with R²=0.99; the sign is lost in extraction, and loss falls with compute. This fit has no Lmin term, unlike the gFID fits. V7 removed: one fixed tokenizer cannot show setup-dependence.

rows.subject: Stage 2 autoregressive image-generation models (Pareto frontier; ImageNet 256x256)
rows.size_stated: Models in the sweep range from 5.21 × 10^7 to 7.75 × 10^8 parameters.
rows.stage_stated: Stage 2 autoregressive generation; independently trained runs, evaluated at their endpoints.
rows.operation_detail: Swept training compute and fit generation FID as a function of compute.
rows.measure: Generation FID versus training FLOPs; Pareto-fit exponent α = −0.65.
rows.value: The paper reports log-log-linear scaling on the Pareto frontier; α = −0.65.
rows.note: The authors describe FID scaling across model scales; the fitted law is for generation FID, not held-out language-model cross-entropy.
rows.check: gFID is not held-out loss, but it follows the same saturating power-law form (C^-0.65·e^25.91 + 2.21, R²=0.99). It bears on V5's power-law form in another modality. V7 removed: this is the single baseline fit, and setup-dependence only appears in the comparisons (R3).

rows.subject: Stage 2 autoregressive image-generation models using the CRT tokenizer (Pareto frontier; ImageNet 256x256)
rows.size_stated: Models in the sweep range from 5.21 × 10^7 to 7.75 × 10^8 parameters.
rows.stage_stated: Stage 2 autoregressive generation; independently trained runs, evaluated at their endpoints.
rows.operation_detail: Swept training compute using causally regularized visual tokens and fit generation FID as a function of compute.
rows.measure: Generation FID versus training FLOPs; Pareto-fit exponent α = −0.73, compared with −0.65 for the baseline tokenizer.
rows.value: CRT scaling exponent α = −0.73; authors report 1.5–3× compute efficiency gains over baseline in the plotted comparison.
rows.uncertainty: R² = 0.99 for both fits, as shown in Figure 7.
rows.note: The paper reports better scaling and lower generation FID for CRT tokens across model scales, despite somewhat worse reconstruction FID.
rows.check: The exponent shift is a comparison between the authors' own tokenizer and the baseline. Keep it for V7 only as evidence that the gFID exponent depends on tokenization (−0.65 to −0.73). The val-loss exponent barely moves (0.255 vs 0.264), which should be noted.

rows.subject: Stage 2 autoregressive image-generation models (aggregate Pareto frontiers)
rows.size_stated: Models in the sweep range from 5.21 × 10^7 to 7.75 × 10^8 parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-scaling behavior after changing the number of tokens per image.

conditions.value: Same base tokenizer evaluated at different sequence lengths: 256, 400, or 576 tokens per image
Compute scaling approaching the reconstruction-FID saturation barrier

rows.measure: Generation FID and compute-efficient sequence length; the paper states shorter sequences are generally more compute-efficient before saturation, while more tokens become compute-optimal near the reconstruction-FID barrier.
rows.value: The compute-efficient choice changes with sequence length and proximity to saturation; the true trend deviates more from the predicted trend as token count increases close to saturation.
rows.note: This is a stated qualitative result about how the scaling trend changes with token count and saturation, not a numerical comparison of individual runs.
rows.check: Partial is for V5: a single power law holds, but the true trend deviates from the extrapolation near the rFID floor at 400/576 tokens. For V7 this is an observed bend away from the fitted law. The fitted exponents are missing: 0.65, 0.54 and 0.58 for 256, 400 and 576 tokens (Figure 5).

rows.subject: Stage 2 autoregressive image-generation models (codebook-size comparison; ImageNet)
rows.size_stated: Models in the sweep range from 3.14 × 10^7 to 7.75 × 10^8 parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Compared generation-FID compute scaling for different stage 1 codebook sizes.
rows.measure: Generation FID comparison across compute scales.
rows.baseline: 131k-code codebook tokenizer; its reconstruction FID is lower than the 1k tokenizer’s.
rows.value: The 1k codebook outperforms the 131k codebook by 5–10 gFID at low compute, despite worse reconstruction FID.
rows.note: The relative outcome changes with compute regime, indicating the scaling comparison depends on tokenizer setup.
rows.check: This is a gFID ordering between tokenizers at low compute, not a power-law form, so V5 is removed. It bears on V7 only through the different fitted curves. The Figure 6 exponents are missing: 0.67 (1k), 0.64 (16k), 0.57 (131k). The text also says the 1k rFID is 'significantly lower', apparently a typo for 'worse'.

rows.subject: Stage 2 autoregressive image-generation models (codebook-size comparison; ImageNet)
rows.size_stated: Models in the sweep range from 3.14 × 10^7 to 7.75 × 10^8 parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Compared generation-FID compute scaling for different stage 1 codebook sizes.

conditions.value: High compute, as stage 2 approaches generation-FID saturation

rows.measure: Generation FID comparison across compute scales.
rows.value: The 131k codebook outperforms the 1k codebook at the high-compute end; the crossover occurs around 10^17 training FLOPs.
rows.note: The ordering reverses relative to the low-compute condition in R5.
rows.check: This is an ordering crossover near 1e17 FLOPs, not a power-law test, so V5 is removed. It shows that the scaling curves for different tokenizers cross.

rows.subject: Stage 2 autoregressive image-generation models (codebook-size comparison; ImageNet)
rows.size_stated: Models in the sweep range from 3.14 × 10^7 to 7.75 × 10^8 parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Compared generation-FID scaling with codebook sizes 1k, 16k, and 131k.
rows.value: The 16k codebook outperforms both other sizes at almost every compute scale.
rows.note: The paper also notes that the 16k tokenizer has worse reconstruction FID than the 131k tokenizer (2.21 versus 1.72).
rows.check: It shows which codebook size gives the best gFID at most compute scales, a tokenizer-selection finding. It says nothing about the power-law form or exponent dependence beyond R5/R6.

rows.subject: Stage 2 autoregressive image-generation models using the baseline tokenizer and CRT tokenizer (aggregate Pareto frontiers)
rows.size_stated: Models in the sweep range from 5.21 × 10^7 to 7.75 × 10^8 parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation-loss scaling curves for baseline and CRT tokenizers.
rows.measure: Validation cross-entropy scaling; the paper says CRT models achieve systematically lower validation losses. Figure 7 reports fitted curves for the two tokenizers.
rows.value: CRT tokenizer curve is systematically lower; exact fitted validation-loss exponents are not stated in the text.
rows.uncertainty: R² = 0.99 for both fits, as shown in Figure 7.
rows.note: A direct result on visual-token validation cross-entropy; not language-model pretraining loss.
rows.check: The exponents are given in Figure 7 (left): CRT 0.264 vs baseline 0.255, both R²=0.99. So 'not stated' is wrong. The CRT val-loss curve also follows a power law in compute. Lower loss for CRT is a comparison of the authors' own method with a baseline, not a scaling-law result.

rows.subject: Stage 2 autoregressive image-generation models using CRT and baseline tokenizers (aggregate across model scales)
rows.size_stated: The hyperparameter-ablation generation-FID average uses stage 2 model scales 52M, 111M, 211M, and 340M.
rows.operation_detail: Compared generation performance across compute and model scales for CRT and baseline tokenizers.
rows.measure: Generation FID versus training compute; authors report CRT improves performance across all tested model sizes and compute settings, with gains especially pronounced at smaller scales.
rows.baseline: Baseline tokenizer scaling curve and generation performance.
rows.value: CRT learns faster and is more performant across all model sizes; authors report 1.5–3× compute efficiency gains in the main text.
rows.note: ImageNet is a finite dataset; the authors describe their stage 2 training as a repeated-data regime.
rows.check: This is the study's own method (CRT) compared with the baseline at each model scale (Figure 13); it is not a scaling-law test. size_stated is wrong: Figure 13 covers all seven scales from 52M to 775M, not the ablation scales.

relationships.condition: Class-conditional AR image generation on ImageNet 256x256, 52M–775M parameters, repeated data, ~4 orders of training FLOPs
relationships.reason: Visual-token val cross-entropy follows a power law in compute (exponent ~0.255–0.264, R²=0.99), and gFID follows a saturating power law (R²=0.99); rows R1, R2, R3, R8.
relationships.display_finding: Validation cross-entropy followed a compute power law with exponent approximately 0.255–0.264 and R²=0.99, while gFID followed a saturating power law with R²=0.99.

relationships.condition: Longer token sequences (400/576 per image) as gFID nears the reconstruction-FID floor
relationships.reason: Authors state the true trend deviates from the fitted extrapolation near saturation, so a single power law fits less well there; row R4.
relationships.display_finding: Generation quality deviated from fitted extrapolations near saturation, weakening the single power-law fit.

relationships.condition: Varying stage-1 tokenizer (causal regularization, tokens per image, codebook size) on ImageNet
relationships.reason: Fitted gFID exponents shift with tokenizer: 0.65 to 0.73 with CRT; 0.54/0.58 for longer sequences; 0.67/0.57 for codebook sizes. Curves cross and bend near saturation; rows R3, R4, R5, R6. Exponent values are from the figures.
relationships.display_finding: Fitted gFID exponents shift from 0.65 to 0.73 with causal regularization, take values of 0.54/0.58 for longer sequences and 0.67/0.57 across codebook sizes, and accompany crossing curves that bend near saturation.
